dossiers.title: RoboCop: Rogue City - Unfinished Business
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 8 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Heavy, deliberate RoboCop movement and the Auto-9 pistol anchor an empowering first-person shooter in which players enjoy throwing enemies, using environmental destruction and responding to differentiated armored enemies.
Most missions climb the confined OmniTower floor by floor, creating a linear focused firefight campaign rather than the original Rogue City's broader Detroit policing and street exploration.

Additional weapons and playable sequences as Alex Murphy or ED-209 add variety, but reused skills, familiar UI and relatively unchanged shooting systems leave some players feeling it resembles standalone DLC.

Early player reports describe crashes, stutter, visual glitches, broken weapon swapping and occasionally lost checkpoint progress; the developer subsequently acknowledged and patched some issues, so July 2025 launch defects do not prove all remain current.
Fans appreciate Peter Weller's RoboCop portrayal, retrospective glimpses of Murphy and ED-209 spectacle, though some describe stiff cinematics and underdeveloped non-combat dialogue.

The concentrated tower premise reduces open-ended investigation and police tasks; repetitive corridors and unavoidable incidental objectives undermine variety for some, while others prefer the more combat-heavy pacing.
New enemy compositions and weapons encourage adapting firepower, but upgraded Auto-9 builds can feel overpowered and lessen the tactical need to switch tools.

A Russian-speaking Steam player recommends the fan service despite visual bugs, while the Steam page lists Russian UI and subtitles but no Russian voice acting; isolated complaints about untranslated snippets should not imply the whole game is unavailable in Russian.

dossiers.title: UBERMOSH
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 8 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: The arcade core is a 90-second top-down survival arena: move through enemy swarms, slash or deflect bullets with a sword, and use dropped firearms to score kills.
Instant restarts, randomly chosen arena palettes and a timed score target make it suited to a few intense minutes rather than lengthy exploration or a story campaign.

Sword-only Kensai, gun-focused Gunner and powerful but fragile Warlock variations change the starting equipment and allowed weapons, providing alternate challenges without persistent character levelling.

High enemy density, small visual field and attacks from all directions require fast reactions; players report constant deaths but often call the learning curve fair once deflection timing is mastered.
Some players describe the repeated short sessions as highly addictive for score chasing, while others find the one principal arena and limited attack repertoire repetitive after a few hours.
Players praise energetic retro cyberpunk pixel art and pumping soundtrack as essential to the appeal, although heavy sensory intensity can become tiring during longer sessions.

A Russian player says the game contains almost no conventional plot or upgrades, with ninety-second rounds feeling surprisingly stressful; this minimalism is a deliberate feature but a weak fit for players who need narrative progress.
A player notes that the compact viewport can make some projectile arrivals feel unfair; others report responsive controls and a straightforward setup with modest hardware demands.

dossiers.title: ULTIMATE MARVEL VS. CAPCOM 3
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 8 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: This fast 3-on-3 tag fighter centers on creating teams, calling assist attacks, switching active members and performing extended aerial combos, with deep synergies among distinct Marvel and Capcom characters.

Players describe a large execution and matchup skill ceiling and sometimes overwhelming extended combos; newcomers may struggle against highly practised opponents despite its immediate audiovisual spectacle.

Longstanding reports of delay-based netcode, region/distance sensitivity and small matchmaking pools remain relevant; people near their friends can fare better, and later players report finding matches via private communities or Parsec.

Roster breadth and the difference between possible three-person team combinations give ample replay for local versus play, but offline modes are limited compared with fighters built around narrative campaigns.

Arcade and the Heroes and Heralds card-collection mode offer structured single-player goals, though there is no RPG-like persistent build progression; the Steam port includes previously released extra content.
Fans praise comic-book styling, crossover character nostalgia and high-energy soundtrack as major enduring attractions, especially for couch sessions with other fighting game players.
Some players criticize balance swings and near-infinite touch-of-death setups; others treat those extreme combos as a core part of the game's competitive identity.

The original title debuted in 2011 while the Steam PC version arrived in 2017; Russian-language Steam feedback is indicated by a small review count, but individual Russian review texts could not be retrieved reliably for semantic inclusion.
